categories.name: Growth plan and market analysis
categories.summary: Knowing where the next patients can come from: how large the reachable market is, who serves it now, what share the practice holds, and a written plan with numbers for the next one to three years.
good_looks_like: The practice can state its market in countable units: residents, beds, facilities, or people in an age group within a travel time.
It knows its main competitors and why referrers choose them.
A written plan names the two or three sources of growth, with volumes, dates and what each requires.
Growth is tracked monthly against the plan.
failure_modes: Growth is whatever happens. Nobody can say whether a good year came from more patients or one-time collections.
The practice chases every opportunity and finishes none.
Volume grows faster than clinician capacity, credentialing or cash.
A decline is noticed only in the bank balance, months after it began.
key_questions: How many potential patients or beds are within our reach, and what share do we serve?
Where did last year's revenue change come from: volume, rate, mix or one-time items?
What are our two main sources of growth for the next 12 months?
What is the limiting factor: demand, clinician time, enrollment or cash?

actions.action: Size the market in countable units
actions.detail: For a facility practice: every facility within a set drive time, its beds and who covers it. For an office: population by age within the service area.

actions.action: Split revenue change into its parts
actions.detail: Volume, payment per visit, payer mix and one-time collections, each year.

actions.action: Write a one-page growth plan
actions.detail: Two or three initiatives, each with a number, a date, an owner and what it needs.

actions.action: Review growth monthly
actions.detail: New patients, active census or panel, visits and collections against plan.

categories.applies_when: Every practice that wants to grow or must replace lost volume: office practices size the market by population, facility-based practices by facilities, beds and who arranges physician coverage. In nursing homes each resident may choose an attending physician (42 CFR 483.10(d)), so a coverage agreement does not guarantee patients.
categories.evidence_note: Planning practice from general business guidance (SBA) and the MGMA body of knowledge, not from measured outcomes. No growth benchmark applies across practices. MGMA polls show how many groups grew in a year, which is context and not a target.

metrics.name: Year-over-year net revenue growth
metrics.definition: Change in net revenue (what the practice actually collected) for a period compared with the same period a year earlier, with one-time collections shown separately.
metrics.formula: (Net revenue this period - same period last year) / same period last year
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable benchmark exists. Context: in MGMA polls of June 2026, 47% of 221 groups reported year-to-date revenue above 2025 and 36% below, while 84% reported higher costs. The practical test is revenue growing faster than operating cost.
metrics.data_hint: The income statement, with a note of any one-time collections.

metrics.name: Share of the target market served
metrics.definition: The practice's patients, beds covered or facilities served as a share of the market it defined as reachable.
metrics.formula: Patients, beds or facilities served / total in the defined market
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Its use is to show how much room remains and whether growth must come from new sites or from deeper share at current ones.
metrics.data_hint: The practice's census, plus Medicare's Care Compare list of nursing homes, the state's licensed facility list, or Census population data by age.

categories.name: Service-line expansion
categories.summary: Adding services that existing patients need and payers cover: care management, wellness visits, advance care planning, transitional care, procedures, diagnostics or telehealth. Usually the cheapest growth, because the patients are already there.
good_looks_like: The practice has listed the covered services its patients qualify for and are not receiving.
Each new service has a written workflow: who is eligible, who does the work, what is documented, how it is billed.
A new service starts small, is audited early, then expands.
Its revenue and cost are tracked on their own line.
failure_modes: A program is billed for most patients before the staff, logs and consent process exist.
A time-based service is billed with no record of the time.
Revenue projections from a vendor selling the program are taken at face value.
The service is added, then quietly lapses because nobody owns it.
Nearly every care-management patient is billed the complex code, which is about 8% of base care-management claims nationally (2024 Medicare data), and the practice stands out to reviewers.
key_questions: Which covered services do our patients qualify for that we do not provide?
For each service we added in the last two years, who owns it and what does it earn?
Has each new service had a chart audit in its first 90 days?
What would the service earn at Medicare rates, after the staff time it needs?

actions.action: List eligible but unserved patients for each candidate service
actions.detail: Annual wellness visits, transitional care after discharge to home or assisted living, chronic care management or the monthly advanced primary care management codes, advance care planning.

actions.action: Write the workflow before the first claim
actions.detail: Eligibility, consent where required, who does what, documentation, code, and frequency limits.

actions.action: Pilot with a small group and audit it
actions.detail: Ten to twenty patients, then an outside review of the records before scaling.

actions.action: Price it honestly
actions.detail: Medicare payment less the staff time and tools it takes, not the vendor's projection.

actions.action: Check self-referral rules before adding tests, imaging, therapy or equipment
actions.detail: Laboratory, imaging, therapy and equipment are designated health services under the physician self-referral law. The in-office exception (42 CFR 411.355(b)) sets who performs the service, where and who bills. Have counsel review vendor-run programs.

categories.applies_when: Any practice with an established patient base. Setting matters: transitional care needs a discharge to home, a domiciliary, a rest home or assisted living, and care management, billable for facility residents, pays roughly a third less where the facility rate applies, such as a hospital or Part A skilled stay.
categories.evidence_note: Coverage rules come from CMS booklets and web pages. CMS's 2025 improper payment data show error rates of 65% for basic chronic care management (99490) and 30% for advance care planning (99497), about nine-tenths from insufficient documentation, so workflow first is well supported.

metrics.name: Share of revenue from services added in the last 24 months
metrics.definition: Collections from services the practice began offering within the past two years, as a share of total collections.
metrics.formula: Collections from services started in the last 24 months / total collections
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. A high share from one new time-based service is a reason to audit it, not only a success.
metrics.data_hint: Collections by code from the billing system, grouped by service.

vendor_refs.note: Sizes care-management, wellness and cognitive-assessment revenue by volume times rate. Wrong that 99483 can be billed with a same-day office visit or advance care planning, and lists retired code G0505.
Section 11 has a sound six-question costing checklist for a new service: start-up cost, ramp, real payer rates, staffing, break-even. Silent on coverage rules, documentation and audits.
Explains self-referral limits on in-office laboratory, imaging and therapy and on vendor turnkey programs. Wrong that the in-office exception needs a group practice: a solo physician qualifies.

categories.name: Referral and facility relationships
categories.summary: Most practices depend on a small number of people who send or assign patients: referring physicians, hospital case managers, facility administrators and directors of nursing. Those relationships are an asset that needs deliberate upkeep.
good_looks_like: The practice knows where each new patient came from.
Each important source has a named contact in the practice and a record of recent contact.
The practice knows what each source values, such as response time or communication with families, and measures it.
No single source accounts for a share of revenue the practice could not survive losing.
Any paid role at a referral source, such as a medical directorship, has a signed agreement, fair market value pay and a log of the time worked.
failure_modes: A facility changes administrator and the new one brings a different physician group.
The owner personally holds every relationship and nothing is written down.
The practice gives gifts, free services or payments to win referrals. For Medicare and Medicaid patients that can be a felony under the Anti-Kickback Statute (42 USC 1320a-7b(b)).
A source stops referring and nobody asks why.
key_questions: Which three sources send us the most patients, and what share of revenue is each?
Who at each source decides, and when did we last speak with them?
What do they want from us that we could measure?
Is anything of value passing between us and a referral source, in either direction?

actions.action: Record the source of every new patient
actions.detail: A required field at intake or admission.

actions.action: Keep a relationship record for each source
actions.detail: Decision makers, last contact, what they want, any agreement and its end date.

actions.action: Agree service standards and report on them
actions.detail: Set your own, for example new residents seen within 72 hours and calls returned within an hour. The federal floor is only a physician visit every 30 days for the first 90 days (42 CFR 483.30(c)).

actions.action: Have counsel review anything of value exchanged with a referral source
actions.detail: Meals, gifts, free staff time and directorship pay fall under the kickback and self-referral rules. Safe harbors (42 CFR 1001.952) expect written terms, fair market value and no link to referral volume.

categories.applies_when: Every practice that receives patients from others. In facility-based practice referrals run both ways: facility leaders steer residents to physicians, physicians admit and order services there, and each resident keeps the right to choose an attending physician (42 CFR 483.10(d)).
categories.evidence_note: The limits on payments to referral sources are federal statute and regulation. States add their own: in Florida, section 817.505 bans paying to induce patient referrals whoever the payer is. Relationship management itself is business practice with no measured benchmark.

metrics.name: Share of new patients from the top three sources
metrics.definition: New patients or revenue from the three largest referral sources or sites, as a share of the total.
metrics.formula: New patients (or revenue) from the top three sources / total
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. A first-principles test, not a published standard: losing any one source should not remove more revenue than the practice's cash reserve can cover for three months.
metrics.data_hint: The referral source field in the billing system, or revenue by site.

metrics.name: New patients per month
metrics.definition: Count of patients seen by the practice for the first time in the month, by source or site.
metrics.formula: Count of first-ever visits in the month
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend.
metrics.data_hint: New-patient and initial-visit codes by month, or first date of service per patient.

vendor_refs.note: Chapter 14 covers a referral log, 24-hour patient contact, reports back to referrers and volume trends by source. Its 70% to 85% conversion target is unsourced. Nothing on facility relationships.
Plain-language screen for leases, directorships, gifts and vendor deals with referral sources. States the 60-day overpayment rule in its pre-2025 form and credits it to the wrong statute.

categories.name: New sites and geographic expansion
categories.summary: Adding an office, a facility or a service area. A site is worth adding when it brings enough volume to justify clinician time and travel, and when the practice can staff it without weakening existing sites.
good_looks_like: Each proposed site has a short case: expected patients, visits, revenue, clinician days, travel and start-up cost.
A named clinician and schedule exist before the practice commits.
The site's payer mix and enrollment needs are checked in advance.
Results are compared with the case at three, six and twelve months.
failure_modes: A site is added as a favor and never reaches enough volume to cover the trip.
Existing sites lose attention and their volume falls by as much as the new one adds.
The new location, including a newly served facility, is not reported to Medicare within 30 days. Failure to report is a ground for revoking enrollment (42 CFR 424.535(a)(9)).
A lease is signed for space the practice's model does not need.
key_questions: How many patients would this site bring in the first three months and at maturity?
Which clinician goes, on which days, and what stops if they do?
Has the location been reported to Medicare (within 30 days) and to every plan?
At what volume does the site cover its cost, and by when?

actions.action: Write a one-page case for each site
actions.detail: Volume, revenue at current yield, clinician days, travel time, start-up cost, break-even month.

actions.action: Set a minimum starting volume
actions.detail: Agree with the facility or referrers on the initial census before committing.

actions.action: Report the new location to Medicare and each plan
actions.detail: Medicare wants each new practice location, including facilities visited, reported within 30 days (42 CFR 424.516(d)). File no more than 60 days ahead or it may be returned. A site in another Medicare contractor's region needs a separate application.

actions.action: Review at three, six and twelve months
actions.detail: Keep, fix or exit, decided against the written case.

categories.applies_when: Practices considering another office, facility or county. For visiting practices travel time is the main cost and each facility counts as a practice location for Medicare, while for office practices the main cost is the lease and front-desk staff.
categories.evidence_note: Enrollment reporting duties are federal regulation and the instructions on Medicare's enrollment forms. Site economics are arithmetic from the practice's own yield and costs, with no published benchmark.

metrics.name: Months for a new site to cover its cost
metrics.definition: Months from opening until a site's collections exceed its direct cost in the same month, including clinician time and travel.
metrics.formula: Count of months from first visit to the first month where site collections exceed site direct cost
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare each site with its own written case, and sites with each other.
metrics.data_hint: Collections and clinician days by site.
metrics.vendor_claim: A second office is worth opening only if it can cover its costs within a year and a half on realistic volume.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is given and none was found. It assumes a leased office and says nothing about visiting practices with little fixed cost.

vendor_refs.note: Section 11 lists tests for a second office and a three-scenario model at 60%, 80% and 100% of target volume. Thresholds are unsourced. Ignores Medicare location reporting and visiting practices.

categories.name: Adding clinicians
categories.summary: Hiring a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant to grow. The decision rests on demand that exists now, the months before payers pay for the new clinician's work, and what the hire does to quality and oversight.
good_looks_like: Unmet demand is measured, such as waiting patients, turned-away facilities, or clinicians above a sustainable visit count.
A hiring case shows cost, expected visits, collections per visit, and the ramp month by month.
Health plan credentialing starts at offer acceptance, the Medicare application is filed within 60 days of the start date, and cash is set aside for the ramp.
The new clinician's charts are audited in the first 90 days.
failure_modes: A clinician is hired on hope and sits half-full for a year.
Health plan credentialing runs late. Medicare can pay back to the application filing date (42 CFR 424.520(d)), but some plans allow no claims for visits before approval.
A nurse practitioner is assigned work that only a physician may do or bill.
The owner's oversight is spread too thin and coding patterns drift.
key_questions: What evidence shows demand for another clinician today?
At how many visits a day does a new clinician cover their full cost?
How many months of that clinician's pay can we carry before collections arrive?
Which visits in our setting must a physician personally perform?

actions.action: Calculate break-even visits a day
actions.detail: Full yearly cost (pay, payroll taxes, benefits, malpractice cover) divided by collections per visit, then by working days. AMGA 2025 medians for pay alone: family physician $342,411, primary care nurse practitioner $149,178.

actions.action: Model the ramp and the cash need
actions.detail: Assume low volume and slow payment for the first three to six months, a planning assumption. Medicare's standard for online applications is 15 to 85 days. Some plans have taken 100 days and allowed no back-billing.

actions.action: Check scope and billing rules for the role
actions.detail: State scope of practice and supervision, Medicare's 85% rate for nurse practitioners and physician assistants (42 CFR 414.52, 414.56), visits reserved for physicians, no 'incident to' billing at the full rate for hospital or skilled nursing patients (42 CFR 410.26).

actions.action: Audit early
actions.detail: Review at least ten of the new clinician's charts in the first month and again at 90 days. OIG's guide for small practices suggests five to ten records per physician as a basic sample.

actions.action: Ask the local hospital about recruitment support for a physician hire
actions.detail: A hospital may fund relocation or guarantee income for a physician who moves into its area and joins the practice. Terms must be written and signed, carry no referral conditions, and pass the money to the physician (42 CFR 411.357(e)).

categories.applies_when: Practices with more demand than clinician time. Delegation has limits: in a skilled nursing facility the physician personally makes the initial comprehensive visit and may delegate only alternate required visits (42 CFR 483.30), and state law sets supervision.
categories.evidence_note: Pay medians are AMGA survey data from mostly large groups. Payment and visit rules are federal regulation. Supervision is state law: in Florida, nurse practitioners need a physician protocol unless registered for autonomous primary care (sections 464.012 and 464.0123). Break-even is the practice's own arithmetic.

metrics.name: Months for a new clinician to cover their cost
metrics.definition: Months from a clinician's start date until the collections from their work in a month exceed their full monthly cost.
metrics.formula: Count of months from start to the first month where attributable collections exceed pay, taxes, benefits and direct costs
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Plan for the enrollment period plus the payment lag. Medicare's contractor standard for online applications is 15 to 85 days (First Coast, 2026). MGMA members reported plans taking up to 100 days (2021 poll).
metrics.data_hint: Collections by rendering clinician and payroll.
metrics.vendor_claim: A new clinician covers their cost after roughly three to nine months, and an experienced nurse practitioner or physician assistant usually within six.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is cited, and the document says it widened its ramp figures to make them agree. Use the practice's own model.

metrics.name: Clinician capacity in use
metrics.definition: Visits actually performed as a share of the visits clinicians could sustainably perform in the period.
metrics.formula: Visits performed / (clinician days x sustainable visits a day)
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark exists. The sustainable number is the practice's own judgment: use above it signals a hire, well below it a demand problem. AMGA 2025 medians: 6,505 work relative value units a year for family physicians, 4,647 for primary care nurse practitioners.
metrics.data_hint: Visits by clinician and days worked.
metrics.vendor_claim: Keep each clinician at 85% to 95% of theoretical visit capacity. Below 80% is revenue to recover and above 95% is an access and retention risk.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is cited. A workable starting band only if the practice sets capacity honestly, including travel time for visiting clinicians.

vendor_refs.note: Section 11 models a new clinician's ramp and monthly cash drain. Its ramp lengths and dollar ranges are unsourced, and a note admits one was widened to reconcile with others.
Backward-planned timeline for enrolling a new clinician with each payer. Says to file Medicare 90 or more days ahead, but applications received over 60 days early may be returned.
Chapter 13 tracks days from start date to first accepted claim, by payer. Its under-60-day target for plans is labelled aspirational, with 90 to 150 days called typical. Both unsourced.

categories.name: Marketing and reputation
categories.summary: How patients, families and referrers find and judge the practice: directory listings, online profiles and reviews, a website, and outreach. For referral-based practices, accuracy matters more than promotion. Healthcare marketing has its own federal rules.
good_looks_like: The practice's name, address, phone, specialty and clinicians are correct in the national provider registry, payer directories and major online listings.
Someone checks reviews and responds without disclosing patient information.
Referrers have a simple way to reach the practice and know what it offers.
Marketing spend is small, tracked, and tied to a source of new patients.
A patient's name, photo or story appears in marketing only with signed authorization (45 CFR 164.508).
failure_modes: A wrong specialty code or address in the national provider registry or a payer file can cause denials, payment delays and misdirected referrals.
A clinician who left years ago is still listed.
A reply to an online review confirms someone is a patient, which discloses protected health information without permission (45 CFR 164.502(a)).
Money is spent on advertising with no way to tell whether it brought anyone in.
Gifts above nominal value, free services or routine copayment waivers are used to attract Medicare or Medicaid patients, or a marketer is paid per patient. Both invite federal penalties.
key_questions: Are our registry and directory entries correct for every clinician and location?
Who reads and answers online reviews?
Can a referrer find our phone number and services in under a minute?
What did we spend on marketing last year, and what came of it?
Does anything we give patients or pay marketers depend on Medicare or Medicaid patients choosing us?

actions.action: Correct registry and directory entries
actions.detail: The national provider registry (changes are due within 30 days, 45 CFR 162.410), each payer's directory and the main online listings, for every clinician. Answer plan verification requests: commercial plans must re-verify every 90 days.

actions.action: Assign someone to reviews
actions.detail: Monthly check. Replies never confirm that the writer is a patient or add any detail of care (45 CFR 164.502). Offer to talk by phone instead.

actions.action: Give referrers a one-page summary
actions.detail: What the practice does, where, how to reach it, and response standards.

actions.action: Track marketing by source
actions.detail: Ask every new patient or referrer how they found the practice.

actions.action: Screen every promotion against the patient-inducement and kickback rules
actions.detail: No routine copayment waivers or gifts above the Inspector General's nominal limit ($15 an item, $75 a year, never cash) to attract Medicare or Medicaid patients (42 CFR 1003.1000). No per-patient pay to outside marketers: no safe harbor covers it.

categories.applies_when: Every practice, at different intensity. Office practices that depend on patient choice need an active online presence, while facility-based practices mainly need accurate listings and direct outreach to the people who arrange coverage.
categories.evidence_note: Registry updates, patient privacy, patient inducements and directory checks are federal law. States add advertising rules: in Florida, false or misleading advertising is a ground for discipline (section 458.331). Promotion itself is business practice with no measured benchmark.

metrics.name: Directory and payer listings that are correct
metrics.definition: Share of the practice's registry, payer directory and major online listings that show the right clinicians, specialty, address and phone.
metrics.benchmark_note: No benchmark exists for a practice's own listings, so 100% is a first-principles target. CMS reviews of Medicare Advantage directories in 2016 to 2018 found errors at 45% to 55% of listed locations. Old data, and it measures plans, not practices.
metrics.data_hint: A quarterly check of the national provider registry, each payer directory and main listings.
metrics.benchmark_typical: 45% to 55% of Medicare Advantage directory locations correct

categories.name: Partnerships and affiliations
categories.summary: Formal relationships that bring patients, revenue or services the practice could not build alone: accountable care organizations, health plans including special needs plans, hospitals, hospices, home health agencies, management services organizations and independent practice associations.
good_looks_like: The practice can say what each partner provides and what it expects in return.
Agreements are written, reviewed by counsel, and state how either side can leave.
Any payment between the practice and a partner that refers patients is at fair market value for real services.
Partnership revenue and effort are tracked.
The practice knows which accountable care organization its tax ID belongs to, what that membership pays, and when it can leave.
failure_modes: Joining an organization that takes a fee or a share of payment and delivers little.
Exclusive terms that block better options later. A tax ID whose visits count toward patient assignment can join only one Shared Savings Program organization (42 CFR 425.306).
Payments that reward referrals in either direction.
Dependence on a partner that can leave on short notice. A Medicare Advantage plan may end a contract without cause on 60 days' written notice (42 CFR 422.202(d)).
key_questions: Which organizations in our market need what we do?
For each current partner, what do we receive and what do we give up?
Could any payment be seen as a reward for referrals?
What happens to our patients and revenue if the partner leaves?

actions.action: Map potential partners
actions.detail: Plans (including special needs plans for facility residents), accountable care organizations, hospitals, hospices and home health agencies that serve the same patients. From 2027 Medicare's LEAD model is aimed at small practices and high-needs patients.

actions.action: Hold two exploratory conversations a year
actions.detail: Learn what they need and what they pay for before proposing anything.

actions.action: Have counsel review every agreement
actions.detail: Exclusivity, termination notice, data sharing, and referral laws. Fees set as a share of revenue need special care: in Florida, split-fee arrangements for referred patients are grounds for discipline (section 458.331(1)(i)).

actions.action: Track results by partner
actions.detail: Patients, revenue and time spent.

actions.action: Price accountable care membership in dollars
actions.detail: From 2027, clinicians in a Shared Savings Program or LEAD organization may bill modifier B2, adding 32% to eligible visits, against 16% for the general modifier. Compare that and any shared savings with the fees and duties.

categories.applies_when: Practices of any size: small practices use partnerships to reach contracts that reward quality and lower cost, and data they could not obtain alone. Facility-based practices suit plans and organizations responsible for nursing home residents, such as institutional special needs plans, but should confirm the 2027 visit modifier covers their codes, since the add-on it replaces was an office-visit code.
categories.evidence_note: Referral law limits are federal regulation. In Medicare's Shared Savings Program, 75% of 476 organizations earned payments for 2024 and physician-led ones saved more per patient than hospital-led ones (CMS, 2025). What reaches a member practice depends on its contract.

metrics.name: Share of revenue that depends on partnerships
metrics.definition: Revenue that would stop if the practice's formal partnerships and affiliations ended, as a share of net revenue.
metrics.formula: Revenue dependent on partnership agreements / net revenue
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Read it as a dependence measure as well as a growth measure.
metrics.data_hint: Revenue by source, mapped to agreements in the contract register.

vendor_refs.note: Section 7 explains hospital recruitment support for a physician joining the practice. One bullet wrongly says support cannot flow through the practice. Nothing on accountable care organizations, plans or hospices.
Half a page: model the finances before a joint venture, hospital or private equity deal, and hire an advisor. No contract terms, legal tests or numbers.

categories.name: Acquiring practices or patient panels
categories.summary: Growing by buying another practice, taking over a retiring physician's patients, or absorbing a facility contract. It is faster than organic growth and carries the seller's problems with it.
good_looks_like: The buyer values the target on earnings after a market wage for clinicians, not on revenue.
Diligence covers coding patterns, receivables, payer contracts, enrollment and compliance history.
The deal is structured so the buyer does not inherit past billing liabilities.
A plan exists for keeping the seller's patients, staff and referral sources.
The price is fair market value for the practice itself, with nothing added for referrals the seller may send afterward.
failure_modes: Paying for revenue that leaves with the selling physician.

Buying the seller's company (a stock purchase) with no protection, and inheriting its billing history. Medicare overpayments must be returned if identified within six years of receipt (42 CFR 401.305).
Enrollment under the new owner is not filed by closing, so claims wait. Medicare pays from the filing date of an approved application, but some plans pay nothing before approval.
The purchase is financed with debt the combined practice cannot carry.
Paying above fair market value to a seller who will keep referring patients, which can be treated as paying for referrals under the kickback statute.
key_questions: How much of the target's revenue depends on the seller personally?
What does public Medicare data show about the target's coding patterns?
Will its payer contracts and facility agreements transfer?
How many years of the target's earnings does the price represent?

actions.action: Value on normalized earnings
actions.detail: Earnings after a market wage for every clinician, with one-time items removed.

actions.action: Run billing and compliance diligence
actions.detail: Code distribution against national Medicare data, aged receivables, payer mix, audits, refunds and enrollment files. Privacy rules allow record review for a practice sale as due diligence (45 CFR 164.501), limited to what is needed.

actions.action: Prefer an asset purchase with protections
actions.detail: Buy the assets, not the company. Hold part of the price in escrow against billing liabilities, and get the seller's commitment to stay through a transition.

actions.action: File Medicare and plan enrollment for the new ownership on time
actions.detail: A Medicare billing number cannot be sold or lent (42 CFR 424.550). Report an ownership change within 30 days. A new tax ID needs a new application, filed no more than 60 days ahead. Ask each plan about contract assignment.

actions.action: Test the financing before signing
actions.detail: Normalized earnings must cover yearly loan payments with room to spare. Lenders using Small Business Administration guarantees require coverage of at least 1.15 and normally 10% of the cost from the buyer (SOP 50 10 8.1).

categories.applies_when: Practices with the management capacity and cash to absorb another, and not while the buyer's own billing or leadership depends on one person. When the target is facility-based, its value rests on facility relationships and residents' choice of physician, neither of which the seller owns or can transfer.
categories.evidence_note: Price evidence comes from broker and research summaries of small transactions, not audited data. Enrollment, overpayment and privacy rules are federal regulation. In Florida, a physician who retires or leaves must notify patients and the board where records are held (section 456.057).

metrics.name: Years to recover the price of an acquisition
metrics.definition: The purchase price divided by the yearly earnings the acquired practice adds after all costs, including a market wage for its clinicians.
metrics.formula: Purchase price / added annual normalized earnings
metrics.benchmark_typical: 3 to 6 years for small primary care practices
metrics.benchmark_note: Equivalent to the earnings multiple paid. Scope Research (2025) reports 3 to 6 times yearly earnings for small primary care practices, underlying deals not shown. Marketplace sales of medical practices, 2021 to 2025, had a median of 2.05 times earnings before owner's pay (Iconic).
metrics.data_hint: The purchase agreement and the acquired practice's results after closing.
metrics.vendor_claim: Primary care practices sell for about 3 to 5 times yearly earnings before interest, taxes and depreciation, and independent practices generally for 2 to 6 times.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Partly supported. Scope Research reports 3 to 6 times for small primary care practices. The library cites no source and never deducts a market wage for the owner.

vendor_refs.note: Seven-area billing diligence list, pre-close timeline and day-one checklist. Treats the 30 to 90 day Medicare enrollment gap as lost revenue, though payment can run from the application filing date.
Lists value drivers and earnings multiples by practice type. Multiples have no source, and earnings are never reduced by a market wage for the owner, which overstates the price.
